verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, upon the Gittith. A psalm, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to be sung upon the Gittith: a song of David.
verses.directors_commentary:
This line is verse 1 in the Hebrew Bible; the KJV prints it as an unnumbered heading and starts counting at "O Lord our Lord", so every verse number below runs one higher than in an English Bible. Do not play it as a title card: it is the stage direction of the whole piece, and it tells you the psalm was meant to be performed, led by a named musician in the Temple service.

The KJV's "upon Gittith" simply transliterates and leaves the question alone, and rightly, because nobody knows what the word means. It is feminine and looks like "of Gath", so Rashi and Metzudat Zion take it as an instrument or tune that came from Gath, the Philistine city. Another old guess, mentioned by Rashi and Ibn Ezra, derives it from gat, a winepress, and reads a vintage song, a tune for the treaders. Ibn Ezra also offers a link to Obed-edom the Gittite, a Levite in David's ark story. Treat it as a musical marker whose sound we have lost. "Choirmaster" for lamnatseach is the safe modern reading of a root meaning to lead or to excel. It names an office, not a rank.

philological_notes.note: A musical term of unknown meaning, appearing only in the headings of Psalms 8, 81 and 84. Feminine adjectival form of Gath, or from gat 'winepress'. The ancient authorities split between an instrument or tune from Gath, a vintage song, and a family of Levites from Gath.
Participle of the piel of nṣḥ, to lead or oversee (Chronicles uses it for foremen of work). In the headings it names the leader of the Temple music.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH our lord, how majestic [is] your name in all the earth, which to-set your splendor upon the heavens.
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, our Lord, how vast is the majesty of your name, spread over all the earth. Your splendor was never kept for the earth alone; you have laid it high above the heavens.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm opens and will close on the same line (verse 10), so the speaker begins in a cry of wonder and returns to it at the end. Play it as an exclamation, not a statement: 'mah' is 'how!' and the line runs on one breath. 'Name' stands for God's presence and reputation as it is known among people, which is why the praise is 'in all the earth'. The KJV 'O Lord our Lord' is the nearest English can get to YHWH 'adonenu, but its capitalization hides that the first word is the divine name and the second an ordinary title of a master; 'excellent' is archaic for 'adir, which means grand, majestic, mighty. KJV 'glory' for hod is acceptable, but hod is a royal word: the splendor of a king in his robes. 'Set above the heavens' is hard to parse because tenah is an odd form. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri take it as an infinitive standing in for the past ('to set' = 'you set'), as in 'merdah' (Ibn Ezra compares Genesis 46:3). Metzudat Zion takes it as an imperfect used for the past ('you gave'). Either way the sense is the same, and the KJV 'hast set' is fair. What the KJV hides is how abrupt the Hebrew is: no verb agrees with 'you'.

philological_notes.note: Majestic, mighty, noble; the root is also the source of hadar (verse 6). Radak ties it to the divine name itself, a four-letter name that is not an adjective yet is 'majestic'.

An irregular form of 'give/set'. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Meiri read it as an infinitive in place of a past tense; Metzudat Zion reads an imperfect used for the past ('you gave'). Compare Jeremiah 14:5 'yaledah ve'azov', which Radak and Meiri cite for the infinitive-for-past usage.
Royal splendor, the dignity of a king. Radak glosses it as might and beauty (ha-koach veha-hadar).

verses.translation_literal: From [the] mouth of babes and nursing-ones you have founded strength, on account of your adversaries, to make cease [the] enemy and [the] self-avenger.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the mouths of babes, of children at the breast, you have laid a foundation of strength: a wall raised against those who stand against you, to bring the enemy to silence, and the one who would avenge himself.
verses.directors_commentary: The hard turn of the psalm: after the vast heavens, the smallest voice. Do not play it as sentimental. The image is martial: 'oz is strength, a stronghold, and 'yasad' is to lay a foundation, as for a building, so the strength is built on infant mouths. Here the KJV 'ordained' blurs it; yasad is 'founded' (YLT) or 'established' (ASV). KJV 'because of thine enemies' is fair, but 'still' in 'still the enemy' is archaic for 'make cease', and the avenger is a mitnaqqem, a reflexive form: someone taking vengeance for himself, which YLT keeps as 'self-avenger'. The tradition splits on who the babies are. Rashi reads olelim as the priests and Levites of the Temple, who grow up in dirt like infants and sucklings (olelim from 'olalti be'afar, Job 16:15), and their praise is the strength. Radak, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take them as real infants: the wonder of birth and nursing is a proof of the creator that silences deniers. Ibn Ezra offers a second reading, the child who begins to speak and so to grasp his maker. Meiri hears in it the teaching of creation to the very young. The Hebrew allows all of these; the plain sense is simply a baby's mouth.

philological_notes.note: Children, small ones. Rashi derives it from 'olalti be'afar (Job 16:15), 'I have thrust my horn in the dust', and reads the Temple's praise as coming from priests and Levites who grow up in dirt like infants; he adds that all small children are called olelim because of that dirt. Metzudat Zion notes that even unborn children are olelim (Job 3:16).
Founded, laid a foundation. Radak makes the image the foundation of a building: nursing is the beginning of the recognition of God's kindness.
The reflexive stem: one who avenges himself. Meiri takes the reflexive to mean one who counts the events of his own life as his own revenge-bringing accidents.

verses.translation_literal: For I see your heavens, [the] works of your fingers, [the] moon and stars which you have established.
verses.translation_dramatic: For when I lift my eyes and look on your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars that you set firmly in their places...
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is a pause with the head thrown back: the speaker looks up, and the sentence hangs, because the answer comes only in the next verse. The Hebrew is a plain 'ki', 'for' or 'when', followed by 'I see', which is lighter than the KJV 'when I consider'; he is not weighing arguments but looking. The 'work of your fingers' is the delicate, skilled craft of a artisan, not a laborer's heavy work of the hand; compare Exodus 8:15 (Hebrew numbering), 31:18 and Deuteronomy 9:10 for other 'finger of God' texts. The sun is missing, which the commentators noticed: Ibn Ezra and Radak say that by day only the sun can be seen, while at night a great host appears, or that the sun is hinted at in 'splendor above the heavens' of verse 2; Radak adds that some think the psalm was spoken at night. The KJV 'ordained' for konanta is again weak; the verb means to fix, make firm, set in place. Moon and stars were also the divinities of the nations around Israel; here they are merely made things, set in place by a creator, which is a quiet piece of polemic.

philological_notes.note: 'Works of your fingers', the craft of skilled work. Ibn Ezra counts ten fingers against ten spheres (seven planetary spheres, the zodiac, a ninth sphere and the throne of glory); Radak repeats his idea. Compare Exodus 8:15 and 31:18 and Deuteronomy 9:10 for 'finger' in other texts.
To set firmly, fix. Radak says the creation words 'made' and 'set firm' argue against those who hold the world to be eternal.

verses.translation_literal: What [is] 'enosh, that you remember him, and [a] son of 'adam, that you attend to him?
verses.translation_dramatic: What is a mortal, that you should hold him in mind? What is a son of Adam, that your eye should turn to him and care for him?
verses.directors_commentary: This is the center of the psalm and its question: small voice, large sky. The two lines say the same thing twice, which is the Hebrew way of lifting a thought: 'enosh and 'ben adam are both simply 'human being', with 'enosh the more frail and mortal word. Radak sets this against verse 2: 'mah adir' was a cry at God's greatness, 'mah 'enosh' is the same 'how' turned toward human smallness; he reads it as praise of the mind of the heavenly bodies, set against which man is nothing. Malbim alone reads the very word 'enosh as meaning smallness, and the weak, mortal creature. KJV 'is mindful of' and 'visitest' are old-fashioned and miss the force: zakar is to remember, to call to mind, and paqad is to attend to, to look in on, as one looks in on the sick, or on a flock; it can be a visit of care, or of reckoning. Meiri takes both verbs as God's providence. The KJV 'man' for 'enosh and 'son of man' for ben adam loses the pairing, and in English 'son of man' has since acquired a heavy load of its own.

philological_notes.note: Mortal, human being; the root has to do with frailty. Malbim reads the word itself as marking smallness. Radak contrasts the 'mah' here with the 'mah adir' of verse 2: one is greatness, the other smallness.
To attend to, look in on, take account of. Metzudat Zion says it is a doubling of 'remember'; Meiri reads both verbs as God's providence over a human being.

verses.translation_literal: And you made him lack a little from God, and [with] honor and majesty you crown him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And yet you have made him lack only a little of God himself, and set on his head, as a crown, honor and majesty.
verses.directors_commentary: The answer arrives as a turn: 'and yet'. The question of verse 5 gets an unexpected reply, not 'nothing' but 'almost God'. The verb is chasar: to lack, to be short of, and in this stem to make someone short of something; the Hebrew has 'you made him lack a little from elohim', which is a measure of distance, not a position of lowness. KJV 'a little lower than the angels' is the most famous mistranslation of the verse: it follows the Septuagint's 'angels' and the tradition of Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David and the Targum, who all read elohim as angels (Ibn Ezra compares Daniel 2:11). The word is the ordinary plural-form word for God or gods, and the ASV 'God', BBE 'gods' and YLT 'Godhead' follow it more closely. Radak ties the nearness to the human soul, which is not a body, as angels are not. The second line is royal: kavod and hadar are royal words of the same family as the hod that verse 2 sets above the heavens (hod and hadar are a stock pair, as in Psalms 96:6 and 104:1). So the human being is crowned with regalia like that of God. 'Ateret is a crown, and te'atterehu is 'you crown him', in the present tense, not the 'hast crowned' of KJV. Malbim distinguishes the two words: kavod belongs to the soul, hadar to the body's outward beauty.

philological_notes.note: 'And you made him lack': a causative of 'lack'. The distance is small ('me'at'). Radak says the lack arises because the soul is in a body; Malbim reads it as the accidental lack of one whose true substance is above.
'From God / gods'. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and the Targum read angels; Ibn Ezra compares Daniel 2:11.
Royal words, close kin to hod in verse 2. Radak places the honor in the soul given to the person; Malbim assigns kavod to the soul and hadar to the body.

verses.translation_literal: You make him rule over the works of your hands; everything you have put under his feet.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have given him rule over the work of your hands. Everything you have set beneath his feet.
verses.directors_commentary:
The coronation has a throne room's logic: a crowned head, then a realm. The verb mashal, "to rule", is the verb of kingship; the KJV's "have dominion" is fine, and echoes Genesis 1:26, 28. Do not play this as a tyrant's boast. The speaker has just stood under the stars wondering why he is remembered at all, and this is gift, not grab: "you make him", "you have put". He is a steward, a deputy.

A surprise for the careful ear: the "works of your hands" is the same phrase as the "works of your fingers" in verse 4, but now fingers have become hands. The heavens are delicate work; the whole realm is solid. "Under his feet" is the old image of a conquered enemy whose neck the king treads on (Joshua 10:24), but it is here applied to creatures, not captives. Ibn Ezra reads the scope narrowly, over the earth alone, while Radak allows that it may reach even the heavens by the human mind that can chart them.

philological_notes.note: Hifil of mashal, to cause to rule. A different verb from 'radah' in Genesis 1:26 but the same idea: delegated kingship.
'Under his feet': a standard image of subjection, usually of defeated enemies. Metzudat David: 'they submit to him'.

verses.translation_literal: Flock and oxen, all of them, and also the beasts of the field,
verses.translation_dramatic: The flocks and the herds, every one; and the wild beasts of the open field too.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker now names the realm, and the order of the list is the order of the farmer's world: first what he owns, then what he must contend with. Tzoneh, "flock" (sheep and goats), is a by-form of the usual tzon, and alafim, "oxen", is an old poetic word otherwise found in Deuteronomy 7:13 ("the increase of your cattle"). Rashi and Radak both flag it. These are the animals that clothed, fed and plowed for every family in the audience: wool, milk, meat, traction. Ibn Ezra notes this is a list by usefulness.

The KJV's "yea" for gam is archaic; the Hebrew is a plain "and also". "Beasts of the field" widens the circle beyond the household to the wild, to lions and wolves and wild oxen, which a shepherd knew he did not truly command. The poet's claim is bold and a little ironic: even those are put under human feet. The final word, sadai, is a poetic by-form of sadeh, "field", as Metzudat Zion notes.

philological_notes.note: A rare by-form of tzon, small livestock (sheep and goats). Compare Numbers 32:24 'tzon'akhem'.
Oxen, cattle (cf. Deuteronomy 7:13 'sheger alafekha', the offspring of your herd).

verses.translation_literal: Bird of the heavens and fish of the sea, passing through [the] paths of [the] seas.
verses.translation_dramatic: The bird of the sky; the fish of the sea; whatever moves along the pathways of the deep waters.
verses.directors_commentary:
The list widens: from the barnyard to the field, now up into the air and down into the sea. This is the creation order of Genesis 1 run in reverse, from the land animals out to the places no one can walk. Radak and Metzudat David read it as human cleverness: the person traps the bird and nets the fish, and builds a ship to sail the sea paths. The poem, however, is more compact than that. It simply says that birds and fish are within the realm.

The KJV's "whatsoever passeth through the paths of the seas" supplies a vague plural noun for a single participle. The Hebrew has "passing through" (over), a singular masculine participle, which could grammatically attach to the fish, "fish of the sea that passes", though the Targum, by adding Leviathan, read it as a separate sea-creature. I keep the participle and the plural "seas": the plural yammim is the old poetic word for the great waters. For an audience on the Mediterranean's edge, the "paths of the seas" were a thing of dread and mystery, the home of chaos monsters in the neighbors' myths. In this psalm they are only roads.

philological_notes.note: 'Paths of the seas': a poetic phrase for the routes through the waters. The plural yammim is an elevated plural, 'the great waters'.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH, our lord, how majestic [is] your name in all the earth!
verses.translation_dramatic: O LORD, our Lord! How vast is your name, how it fills the whole earth!
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain returns, word for word, minus the last clause of verse 2. The audience hears the same line, and it must sound new. The first time it was a shout of wonder before the argument; now it is the answer to the question "what is man?". The poem has moved from God's name to man's crown and back, and the human being's greatness turns out to be a reason to praise God, not to praise man. The psalm ends with no flourish and no petition. Radak says the speaker returns to thanks after finishing the account of what was given to humankind. Ibn Ezra adds that this is true in every generation, because the earth always stands.

Play the repeat quieter and closer. The KJV's "excellent" and "O Lord our Lord" still mislead in the same way as in verse 2: the divine name is YHWH, and the second word is a title, "our master".
